Puro Sound Labs PuroBasic Headphones Review – What's Good To Do

# Puro Sound Labs PuroBasic Headphones Review 

21/12/2019

We have got so used to everything being wireless these days, from our internet connections to the way we charge our phones and speaker systems in our homes. The kids have each got a pair of wireless Puro headphones which they really do love…when they remember to charge them! It doesn’t happen very often, but if they do run out of charge the kids can get very frustrated and more to the point, I end up with a headache as they seem to feel the need to out-sound each other with the volumes of their devices. So, if you’re the kind of person who might forget to charge their headphones or even if you just prefer wired devices and don’t want to have to worry about pairing and which tablet is connected to which set of headphones, having a good, basic wired pair of headphones is a must. 

Because we have been so impressed with the wireless Puro Sound Labs headphones we have had in the past, they were an obvious choice when it came to looking for a wired pair for the kids. We were looking for similar features in a wired pair to a wireless one – we wanted them to be padded, comfortable, adjustable and, most importantly, sound limited. As I said before, both of the kids seem to have a habit of blasting their devices as loud as they possibly can, so having a sound limiter on the headphones is an absolute must for us. 

I was delighted to see that the PuroBasic headphones from Puro Sound Labs ticked all of these boxes and more! They are sound limited to 85db as well as having a leather padded band and ear pads. They are fully adjustable and very comfortable to wear, but the features don’t end there! On the cable is a volume controller as well as mic and a button for answering calls (yes, it even operates as a hands-free set too!). The cable is a strengthened, braided one for extra durability and the 3.5mm jack at the end is the elbow type, which we find far more robust than the straight ones. The headphones even come with their own carry pouch for portability, and they fold up neatly to make them more compact. 

Because they aren’t wireless, they require no setting up, charging or pairing at all – you plug them in and they work! Puro make these in blue, red, green and pink so there will be a colour for every child. We were sent the red ones and the kids both thought they were a lovely, bright colour. I have to say that I was really impressed with both the comfort and the sound of these headphones. They fitted the heads of the adults we tried them on as well as my 10-year-old and 7-year-old; I would suggest they would be perfect for any child aged 5 or over. 

The sound quality they offer is crystal clear, and they are perfectly loud enough, even with the sound limiters. I feel much better knowing the kids’ ears are protected and both kids have said that they are really comfy to wear. They won’t replace our wireless headphones as we have got too used to being wire-free, but they are a fantastic standby for us and for younger kids, for whom you might not want to invest a lot of money in a wireless pair, they would make a fantastic first pair of great quality but inexpensive headphones. They would also be a fantastic addition to the Christmas list of a younger child, especially if they have been lucky enough to have received their first tablet this Christmas! 

Rating: 5/5

RRP: £19.99

For more information visit purosound.com. Available to buy from Amazon here.

our impression is the PuroBasic is a wired, on-ear headphone for kids with one headline capability: a hard 85 dB volume cap. Everything else about it is deliberately minimal, and that simplicity is both the point and the main limitation. Here’s what the specs actually mean when a kid is wearing these for a school day or a long car ride. Fit, Size, and Weight The listed weight is 0.33 kg, which works out to roughly 11.6 ounces. For an on-ear headphone aimed at children, that’s on the heavier side. Light plastic kids’ headphones often land well under 8 ounces, so this is closer to what you’d expect from an adult headphone. For everyday listening. The adjustable headband and plush ear cushions help distribute that weight, but a smaller child may feel it after A hour or two. The data doesn’t specify a recommended age beyond “Kid. ” so if you’re buying for a four- or five-year-traditional, the fit may be a gamble. Older elementary and middle school kids are a safer bet. The on-ear design matters here too. On-ear cushions press against the ear rather than surrounding it, which keeps the headphone smaller and easier to pack but puts more pressure on the outer ear. The soft, breathable cushions are meant to offset that, and the adjustable headband lets you dial in the clamp. Still. If your kid is sensitive to pressure or wears glasses, an over-ear design is generally more ergonomic for long sessions. The rounded earpiece shape is a cosmetic detail more than a functional one. Materials and Build The frame is plastic, described as rugged and flexible. Flexible plastic is the right call for kids-it bends instead of snapping when it gets shoved into a backpack. That said. “plastic” covers a wide range, and the spec sheet doesn’t tell you the wall thickness or hinge quality. The folding ear cups are a practical addition; folding flat makes them easier to store and less likely to get crushed in transit. In real-world use, the included drawstring bag is soft material, which protects against scuffs but not against a heavy textbook landing on top of it. The bag is for organization, not real impact protection. The 1-year warranty is worth noting. That’s a standard term, not a generous one, and it tells you the manufacturer expects typical wear rather than abuse. For a kids’ product that will get tossed around. One year is the minimum you’d want. If your child is hard on gear. Factor in the possibility of replacing these within a couple of years. For most people, the Volume Limiter: What 85 dB Actually Means This is the core of the product. 85 dB is the commonly cited threshold for safe listening over extended periods. For reference, normal conversation sits around 60 dB* (based on available data), a busy classroom or city traffic around 70-80 dB, and a loud movie theater or a lawnmower around 90 dB* (based on available data). Capping output at 85 dB means your kid can’t crank the volume to a level that risks hearing damage during a long session-which is exactly the scenario you’re worried about when a child is wearing headphones for A hour of online class and then another hour of videos. The trade-off is real, though. An 85 dB ceiling is quiet enough that in a noisy environment-a car, a bus, a crowded cafeteria-your kid may struggle to hear dialogue over the background noise. Because the limiter is built in. There’s no override, so you can’t temporarily raise it for a noisy moment. That’s the whole point of the attribute, but it’s the thing to think through before buying. If your child mostly uses these in a quiet house or classroom, 85 dB is plenty. If they’re frequently in loud spaces. They’ll be asking you why everything sounds faint. One more thing the specs make clear: the limiter is the safety mechanism, and there’s no app, no password, no parental control beyond the hardware cap. That’s simpler and harder to defeat than software. Which is a genuine advantage for younger kids. An older kid who wants to listen loud will simply be stuck at 85 dB, and some will find that frustrating. Audio Performance The driver type is listed as a balanced armature. That’s unusual for a kids’ headphone at this level-balanced armature drivers are common in in-ear monitors and tend to be productive and detailed in the mids and highs, but they can lack the low-end punch of a dynamic driver. The frequency range is the standard 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz, which covers the full range of human hearing on paper. In practice, a balanced armature in an on-ear kids’ headphone is likely to sound clear for speech and vocals-solid for online classes and audiobooks-but may not deliver thumping bass for music and games. The impedance is 32 ohms, which is low enough that a phone, tablet, or laptop will drive these easily without a separate amp. You won’t need to worry about volume headroom from the source device; the limiter is the bottleneck, not the power. Passive noise cancellation is listed, which means the ear cushions physically block some outside sound. In practice, it’s not active noise cancellation we could see what we appreciate is -there’s no battery or electronics for that-so don’t expect silence on a plane. It’s the ordinary isolation you get from a closed on-ear cup. Which helps a bit in a noisy room but won’t transform a loud environment. Controls and Connectivity The connectivity is wired only, via a 3.5 mm jack. That’s a deliberate choice for kids: no pairing, no charging, no Bluetooth dropout, and no battery to die mid-class. Plug it in and it works. The flip side is that these are useless with a phone that has no headphone jack unless you supply an adapter, and the spec sheet doesn’t mention one in the box. If your kid’s tablet or school laptop has a standard headphone port, you’re fine. If it’s a newer phone, budget for a dongle. The built-in microphone handles calls and online classes. Wired mics on a 3.5 mm connection are generally trustworthy for voice. Though the spec sheet doesn’t give microphone sensitivity or noise rejection, so I can’t tell you how clear it sounds in a noisy room. For typical video calls and classroom participation, it should do the job. The control type is listed as volume control with a touch control method. That’s a slightly confusing pairing in the data-touch controls on a wired kids’ headphone usually mean an inline remote on the cable rather than touch-sensitive ear cups. The cable is described as retractable, which is a nice practical touch for storage and reduces tangling. I’d treat the “touch” label as referring to the inline controls, but the spec sheet isn’t precise enough to be certain, and that’s worth knowing before you buy if button feel matters to you. Compatibility The compatibility list is broad: anything with a standard 3.5 mm connection, including phones, tablets, laptops, desktops, gaming consoles, smart speakers, and TVs. That universality is the strength of a wired headphone. It’ll work with a school Chromebook, an old iPad, a Nintendo Switch, and a plane’s seat-back entertainment system without any configuration. For a family that wants one pair of headphones to move between devices, that’s genuinely useful. The retractable cable and foldable design support that portability. What’s in the Box and What’s Missing The box contains the headphones and a drawstring bag. That’s it. No 3.5 mm adapter, no splitter for sharing, no spare cable. The bag is soft, so it’s for keeping things tidy rather than protecting against drops. The carrying case material is listed as soft material. Which confirms it’s a pouch, not a hard shell. The data doesn’t give a battery life because there’s no battery-these are passive wired headphones. It also doesn’t specify the cable length, which matters if your kid is using them at a desktop. And there’s no stated age range beyond “Kid. ” so sizing is something you’ll have to judge from the adjustable headband and the 0.33 kg weight. On the practical side, the Review Signal The rating sits at 4.2 out of 5 across 1,380 reviews. That’s a solid but not first-rate score-consistent with a product that does its core job (safeguarded volume, durable enough, works everywhere) but has some complaints mixed in. The best-seller rank in over-ear headphones is respectable but not top-tier, which fits a niche kids’ product rather than a mass-market one. Without reading the individual reviews. The aggregate tells you most buyers are satisfied, but a meaningful minority aren’t. The most likely sources of dissatisfaction, based on the specs, are the on-ear comfort over long sessions, the weight for smaller kids, and the volume ceiling being too quiet in noisy settings. Summary: The PuroBasic is a straightforward wired kids’ headphone built around a fixed 85 dB volume cap, with a foldable plastic frame, a built-in mic, and universal 3.5 mm compatibility. ## Overview

The Puro Sound Labs PuroBasic Kids Wired Headphones are built around one straightforward priority: keeping young ears safe without asking parents to spend a fortune. Puro Sound Labs has made hearing protection the centerpiece of their brand, and that philosophy shows up immediately in the design choices here. At just five ounces, these kids headphones sit lightly on a child's head, and the wired-only, on-ear setup keeps things refreshingly simple. A drawstring carrying bag is tucked into the box — a small but genuinely useful touch for school bags and travel kits. Just don't expect audiophile-grade sound; this is a practical, safety-first headphone for everyday family life.

## Features & Benefits

The headline feature is the built-in 85dB limiter, and it is not a software cap that an app update could quietly override — it is baked into the hardware. Pediatric audiologists generally point to 85 decibels as the threshold where prolonged exposure starts causing damage, so having that ceiling locked in gives real reassurance. The adjustable headband and padded ear cushions handle comfort well enough for a long school day or car ride. Folding the ear cups flat takes about two seconds, and the included bag keeps them scratch-free in a backpack. The integrated microphone works solidly for video calls and remote learning. One honest note: the 3.5mm jack means no Bluetooth pairing, which is a trade-off worth knowing upfront.

## Best For

This wired headset for children is a natural fit for school-age kids — roughly ages three through ten — who use tablets or Chromebooks for learning. If your household runs on multiple devices, the universal 3.5mm connection is a genuine advantage: plug in and go, no pairing screens, no dropped connections mid-lesson. Parents who worry about volume exposure but still need a functional headphone with a mic will find this hits that balance well. The foldable design travels cleanly; it fits in a standard backpack pocket without fuss. That said, households already accustomed to wireless headphones should factor in the cord — kids will yank it, and that is just the reality of wired audio for this age group.

## User Feedback

Parents consistently land on two things they appreciate about the PuroBasic: the volume cap actually works as advertised, and the fit holds up through a full school day without complaints from kids. Those are meaningful wins. On the critical side, audio quality draws the most candid feedback — it is clear and functional, but nobody is calling it rich or immersive. A few reviewers with younger, more active toddlers mention that the hinge points can weaken over time if the headphones get tossed around regularly. The built-in microphone earns generally positive marks for classroom calls, though it is not broadcast-quality. Headband sizing gets occasional mention too — most kids find a comfortable fit, but the range may feel snug on larger heads.

#### Pros

- The hardware-level 85dB volume cap gives parents genuine, reliable hearing protection without relying on software settings a child could change.
- At five ounces, these kids headphones are light enough that most children forget they are wearing them after a few minutes.
- The adjustable headband and padded cushions hold up comfortably across long school sessions and car rides without pressure complaints.
- Foldable ear cups and an included drawstring bag make packing and storing them genuinely effortless.
- The built-in microphone works well enough for remote learning, video calls, and casual gaming voice chat.
- A universal 3.5mm jack means they connect instantly to virtually any device a child is likely to use at school or home.
- The flexible plastic frame has enough give to handle drops and rough handling without snapping under normal kid use.
- No charging, no pairing, no connectivity troubleshooting — plug in and it works every single time.
- The price point makes these a low-stakes purchase for a first headphone or a school backup pair.

#### Cons

- The wired cord is a daily management issue for active younger children who move around constantly.
- Audio quality is functional but flat — music sounds thin, and there is little bass to speak of.
- The 85dB hardware cap can feel too quiet in louder environments like airplanes or busy classrooms.
- Hinge points on the folding ear cups may weaken with heavy-handed use, especially among toddlers.
- The headband adjustment range may feel snug on larger-headed children or slim on very small toddlers.
- No Bluetooth option exists — households accustomed to wireless audio will find the cord a step backward.
- The microphone picks up some ambient noise and is not well-suited for anything beyond basic calls or classroom use.
- The on-ear fit, rather than over-ear, may cause discomfort during very long listening sessions for some kids.
- The carrying bag, while convenient, offers minimal padding and does not protect against hard impacts in a crowded backpack.

## Ratings

The scores below reflect an AI-driven analysis of verified global user reviews for the Puro Sound Labs PuroBasic Kids Wired Headphones, with spam, bot-generated feedback, and incentivized reviews actively filtered out to ensure the results are trustworthy. We evaluated thousands of real parent and caregiver experiences across school, travel, and home use scenarios, then translated those into category-level scores. Reviewers frequently mention recommending these kids headphones specifically because of this feature.

A small number of parents noted that 85dB can feel noticeably quiet in louder environments like airplanes or bustling classrooms, occasionally prompting kids to remove the headphones rather than struggle to hear clearly.

# PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200: Kids’ Headphones Comparison

By Cecilia Yeung Published October 15, 2026

Which headphones should you get for your child: PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200? This comparison guide will take a deep look at these three popular Puro Sound Labs headphones and select the best one for you.

Choosing a pair of decent headphones is not easy. Choose one for kids is even more daunting. That’s why many parents go with a known brand such as Puro Sound Labs who specializes in volume-limiting headphones that are suitable for kids.

Let’s start by knowing some basics about PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200, and then compare them side by side. You can also jump to our product review section to get a whole picture.

## Our Final Verdict

### Winner: PuroQuiets Noise Cancelling Headphones 

It offers active noise-canceling, can be wireless, and has a long battery life

### Best Stylish: BT2200 Volume Limited Headphones 

### Best Basic: PuroBasic Volume Limiting Wired Headphones

It must be wired, avoids Bluetooth radiation exposure, and is inexpensive

## What Are Volume Limited Headphones?

Volume limited headphones or earbuds restrict the maximum volume the listening device can set to. In simple words, volume-limiting headphones cannot play music at a very high volume.

That means even if you set your computer, phone, or tablet to the maximum sound volume, there is still a limit on how loud your headphones can play the sound.

## Why Choose Volume Limited Headphones for Kids?

Why would someone need volume-limited headphones? Well, according to the CDC, long exposure to loud noises can damage ear cells and even cause hearing loss.

The danger is that this doesn’t happen overnight but gradually. That’s why kids who don’t fully understand the harmful effect of loud noises are at higher risk of impairing their heading abilities.

Volume limited headphones are mainly designed for kids and teenagers who love music or need to use headphones for online classes for an extended period of time. The restriction on the volume can prevent damage to the ear membranes 

## Who is Puro Sound?

Puro Sound is a company that specializes in making kids’ friendly headphones. The founder Niki Russell suffered noise-induced hearing loss and is partially deaf. 

The personal experience of the founder motivated her to start this brand to help other kids avoid preventable hearing loss. Puro Sound currently has two collections of headphones for kids: Volume-Limiting Headphones and Hearing Protection.

## Why Choose Between PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200? 

Among all Puro Sound volume-limiting headphones, PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200 are the most popular ones. 

If your child has a preference on the type of connection, the color, and the appearance of the headphones, you should be able to find a great choice among PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200.

## How to Compare PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200?

Though PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200 are all volume-limiting headphones that can help protect kids’ hearing, they have some major differences. So how do you evaluate them? Here are some tips:

- Types of Connection. The key point to check here is whether the headphone is wired or wireless, whether it has Bluetooth, what types of audio cable it uses.
- Hear Protection. You want to check what is the maximum volume that the headphones allow. According to deafblind.org, the suggested volume is between 60 to 85 decibels.
- Microphone. If your child also uses the headphones to record or take interactive training, it’s important to have a built-in microphone.
- Battery Life. If the headphones are wireless, you also need to check how long it takes to charge the headset and how long the battery can last.
- Noise Cancelling Feature. The noise-canceling feature helps reduce unwanted ambient sounds so that you can listen to music in a noisy environment without raising the volume. 
- Accessories. Does the headset offer a case, does it come with the necessary cables? If not, how much does it cost to get extra add-ons?
- Syle and Color. PuroBasic vs PuroQuiets vs BT2200 have many color options. If your child is particular about the look and design of the headphones, it’s a good idea to check the color options first.
